title: Real FreeRTOS on Linux: a sump pump controller

milestones.title: Boot the kernel: a drift-free sensor and a clean exit
milestones.body:
Get the real kernel running and make it do one thing right.

**One task prints.** On the POSIX port, `printf` from several tasks can hang the program (the README explains why). So exactly one *logger* task prints. Every other task sends it a `log_line_t` by value through a queue of `LOG_QUEUE_LEN`, and the logger prints each line as `<tick> <text>`.

**The sensor.** A sensor task samples the tank every `SENSOR_PERIOD_MS` (100 ms) with `hw_read_level()` and logs:

```
100 SENSOR level=502
200 SENSOR level=604
```

The tick on the line is the tick the sample was **due**. A conversion takes 2 to 6 ms, and its length varies, but the samples must stay on an exact 100 ms grid for the whole run, with no drift. The board measures when each conversion starts, so the tests can tell.

**The end.** After `hw_run_ms()` ticks (`--run-ms`, default 3000), log `END` as the very last line. Then the program must exit with status 0, by returning from `main()` or calling `exit()`, so the board can print its `hw: ...` report.

```
$ ./build/plant --run-ms 500
100 SENSOR level=502
200 SENSOR level=604
300 SENSOR level=706
400 SENSOR level=803
500 END
```

Lines with other tags are fine (handy for debugging): the tests ignore tags they don't check. The types are in `src/plant.h`. The tasks, their priorities and how you split the code into files are up to you.

**Done when** `make test-m1` is green.
hints: If the sensor waits 100 ms after a conversion that took 4 ms, when does the next sample start? And when the run is over, how does a program that is running inside vTaskStartScheduler() get back out of it?

Drift-free periods are the absolute-deadline delay from Periodic tasks with vTaskDelayUntil, with the wake time kept from one call to the next. One printing task fed by a queue of structs is the gatekeeper pattern from Queue-driven architecture. FreeRTOS tasks & the API covers creating tasks, priorities and starting the scheduler. The POSIX port supports vTaskEndScheduler(), which makes vTaskStartScheduler() return in main.

In main: hw_init, create the log queue, create the logger and the sensor task, start the scheduler. The sensor loops: wait until the next period, read the level, and send a line stamped with the wake time. Something waits hw_run_ms() ticks and sends a final line marked last. When the logger has printed that one, it flushes stdout and ends the scheduler, and main returns 0.

milestones.title: A control task, a queue and a shared status
milestones.body:
Now the pump.

**Readings travel by queue.** Every sample also goes, as a `reading_t` by value, through a queue of `READING_QUEUE_LEN` to a **control task**. The control task runs the pump with hysteresis:

- the pump is off and a reading is **≥ `LEVEL_HIGH_MM`** (700): switch it on;
- the pump is on and a reading is **≤ `LEVEL_LOW_MM`** (300): switch it off;
- anything else: leave it as it is.

Every switch logs one line, with the level of the reading that caused it:

```
300 SENSOR level=706
306 PUMP on level=706
...
800 SENSOR level=206
806 PUMP off level=206
```

With the right control, the tank never overflows and the pump never runs dry. The board counts both.

**A shared status.** The control task keeps the `plant_status_t` from `plant.h` up to date: samples handled, last and highest level, pump state, number of pump starts. Every read or write of it goes through **one mutex**. Hold the mutex for an update or a copy, never while logging or waiting on something else.

**A richer END.** The END line now reports the status, read under the mutex:

```
2950 END samples=29 pump_starts=3 max_level=706
```

Write the values as `key=value` pairs. Their order doesn't matter, and extra keys are fine.

**Done when** `make test-m2` is green (and m1 still is).
hints: What does the control task need to remember between two readings to know whether the tank is filling or draining? Who else looks at the status, and what could they see if they read it halfway through an update?

A queue copies the struct (Queue-driven architecture), so the sensor can reuse its local reading straight away. The status is the Mutexes & priority inversion lesson, with xSemaphoreCreateMutex(), which has priority inheritance built in. Copy under the lock, then do the slow part outside it, like the boss's telemetry fix.

Sensor: after logging, send the reading to the readings queue. Control: block on the queue, then take the mutex, update the counters, decide on or off from the current pump state and the two thresholds, switch the pump if the decision changed, and give the mutex back. Log the PUMP line after releasing it. The END line copies the whole status under the mutex and formats it outside.

milestones.title: The e-stop interrupt
milestones.body:
`--estop-at T` makes the board press the emergency stop at tick T. Like every real button, its contacts **bounce**: the interrupt fires three times, at T, T+1 and T+3. Attach your ISR with `hw_estop_attach_isr()`.

**The ISR does the minimum.** It counts the edge, remembers the tick of the first edge, and wakes a task with a **task notification**. Only `...FromISR` APIs are allowed in it. The woken task must run **as soon as the ISR returns**, not at the next tick. The board checks whether the pump is already off by the time your ISR has returned to the task it interrupted.

**The woken task makes the plant safe.** It switches the pump off and latches `estop` in the status. From then on the pump must never come back on, so the control task must respect the latch. The sensor keeps sampling and logging as before.

Log exactly **one** line for the stop, however many edges arrive:

```
1537 ESTOP irq=1537
```

`irq` is the tick of the first edge. The END line gets one more key, `estop_irqs=<edges counted>`. That's 3 in the tests.

```
$ ./build/plant --run-ms 2000 --estop-at 1537
...
1500 SENSOR level=507
1537 ESTOP irq=1537
1600 SENSOR level=538
...
2000 END samples=19 pump_starts=2 max_level=839 estop_irqs=3
```

**Done when** `make test-m3` is green.
hints: What's the least an ISR can do and still get the pump off quickly? And if an ISR wakes a high-priority task without asking for a context switch, which task runs when the ISR returns?

Notifying from an ISR, the xHigherPriorityTaskWoken flag and portYIELD_FROM_ISR are in FromISR & portYIELD_FROM_ISR and Task notifications. xTaskGetTickCountFromISR reads the tick inside an ISR. A counter written by an ISR can't be protected by a mutex: make it volatile and only write it in the ISR (Interrupts & ring buffers).

ISR: count the edge, note the tick on the first one, notify the safety task and hand the woken flag to portYIELD_FROM_ISR. Give the safety task a priority above everything else, including the timer daemon. It waits for its notification, takes the mutex, latches estop, switches the pump off, releases, and logs ESTOP only the first time. Control checks the latch inside the same locked section where it would switch the pump on.

milestones.title: Heartbeat and watchdog
milestones.body:
A controller that stops sampling but leaves the pump running will drain the sump and burn the pump out. Catch it.

**The timer.** Create an auto-reload software timer with a period of `WATCHDOG_PERIOD_MS` (250 ms). The sensor task **checks in** once per completed sample. On each expiry, the callback takes the number of check-ins since the last expiry and resets it to zero, as one atomic step. Then:

- one or more check-ins: log `HEARTBEAT checkins=<n>`;
- none: the watchdog **trips**. Log `WATCHDOG sensor stalled`, switch the pump off, and latch `fault` in the status, so the control task never switches it on again. It trips only once. Empty windows after the trip log nothing.

The callback runs in the timer daemon task, so it must never block: not on a queue, not on the mutex.

`--sensor-stall-at T` makes `hw_read_level()` never return from tick T on, the way a dead SPI sensor would.

```
$ ./build/plant --run-ms 2400 --sensor-stall-at 1350
...
1250 HEARTBEAT checkins=3
1300 SENSOR level=706
1306 PUMP on level=706
1500 HEARTBEAT checkins=1
1750 WATCHDOG sensor stalled
2400 END samples=13 pump_starts=2 max_level=706 estop_irqs=0
```

The tests check the heartbeat's timing and counts, that a stall trips the watchdog within two windows, and that the pump goes off before it runs dry.

**Done when** `make test` passes as a whole.
hints: What proves the plant is being controlled: that the CPU is running, or that the sensor task is completing cycles? And what could go wrong if the sensor incremented the counter between the callback reading it and clearing it?

Auto-reload timers, and the rule that callbacks run in the Tmr Svc daemon and must never block, are in Software timers & the daemon task. Reading and clearing in one step is a critical section (Races & critical sections, and the boss lab's watchdog). The Toyota story in Heaps, static allocation & stack overflow is why the check-in comes from the task doing the work.

Create the timer before starting the scheduler, auto-reload, and start it. The sensor increments a counter after each good sample. The callback reads and zeroes it inside a critical section, logs a HEARTBEAT if it was nonzero, and on the first empty window logs WATCHDOG without waiting for queue space and asks the safety task to shut down (a second notification bit works). The safety task latches fault and switches the pump off under the mutex, as it does for the e-stop.
